newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE-Japan wants expanded WTO agenda, info deal.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Japan wants expanded WTO agenda, info deal.

text.p: Japan, long a loud cheerleader for the world free trade system, wants to see the World Trade Organisation expand its agenda to include investment and competition policy when member ministers meet next week.

Japanese official said Tokyo is also keen to see progress at the Singapore meeting toward a global agreement on eliminating tariffs on products in the $500 billion world information technology market.

But with Japan's Trade Minister, Shinji Sato, trapped at home to deal with a domestic scandal and the attendance of the country's foreign minister uncertain, doubts exist over how much political leadership Tokyo can exert to settle sharp differences over such contentious issues.

Ministers from the Geneva-based global trade regulatory body will meet in Singapore on December 9-13 to confirm their commitment to open up their nations' markets and set the agenda for the WTO into the 21st century.
JAPAN WANTS INVESTMENT AND COMPETITION ON WTO AGENDA

Japan and Canada, backed by the European Union (EU), are leading a push to start talks in the WTO on global rules for the treatment of foreign investment, but key developing Asian countries oppose such discussions.
The EU wants an accord to start talks at the WTO on national competition policies. Japan agrees, but argues this should include anti-dumping measures, or special tariffs.

"On these two issues (investment and competition policy) we have been quite keen to see agreement in Singapore so that the WTO can start working on these two items in the future," a Japanese diplomat told Reuters.
Vice Trade Minister for International Affairs Hisashi Hosokawa said on Wednesday that a decision should be made to set up a WTO working party on investment.

"However, several countries still strongly oppose it on the grounds that starting such analytical work may mean eventual negotiations of rules," Hosokawa said. "Having said all this, this issue will remain the most difficult one among those which are expected to produce tangible results."
TOKYO DECLINES TO BACK U.S. ON WORK STANDARDS

On the thorny issue of linking labour standards and trade -- a U.S. proposal strongly opposed by many developing economies -- Tokyo has declined to back Washington but appears to hope some middle ground can be found.

"Our position is that we don't think that the WTO is the right place to take this up, but at the same time we understand the political reality in certain other countries like the United States and some European countries, where there is the perception that trade liberalisation is not bringing benefits to some of their workers," the Japanese diplomat said.

"We are not against discussing the issue in Singapore and not against some reference in the ministerial declaration, but are against formal inclusion...as a subject of the WTO's future agenda," he added.
DECLARATION LEFT TO MINISTERS TO THRASH OUT
Envoys to the WTO last Friday in Geneva dropped efforts to agree on the ministerial declaration. The final text looks likely to be left to the ministers themselves to thrash out.

Emerging economies and poorer developing states believe the big powers are trying to pry open their markets for massive penetration by big multinational corporations at the expense of local firms and investors.

They fear any discussion of work conditions, investment rules and competition policy would lead to binding rules that would leave them open to WTO-approved trade retaliation by the big powers such as the United States, Europe, Canada and Japan.
TOKYO SEEKS PROGRESS ON INFO-TECH DEAL

Tokyo also hopes for progress on a U.S.-led plan to eliminate tariffs on information technology products like microchips and computers by the turn of the century -- the Information Technology Agreement (ITA).

Asia-Pacific leaders at their annual summit in the Philippines last month fudged support for the plan, calling on the WTO "to substantially eliminate tariffs by the year 2000" but at the same time recognising the need for "flexibility".

"Concerning the ITA, it is difficult to predict how far we can go in pulling this together," another Japanese official said. "First there should be agreement among the Quad partners (Japan, the United States, the European Union and Canada). There will need to be more negotiations in Singapore."
TOKYO'S BARGAINING POWER IN DOUBT
Tokyo has long touted the importance of the WTO as the best forum for settling disputes which have bedevilled its economic ties with trade partners like the United States.
But how much influence Japan will have at the Singapore gathering remains to be seen.

Trade Minister Sato said on Thursday he would not be able to attend. Instead, he must stay home and face tough questions in parliament about a scandal linking his bureaucrats to an oil dealer arrested for suspected tax evasion.
Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda has yet to finalise his own plans to attend the meetings, but his appearance is likely to be brief given the demands of parliamentary business.

"It (Japan's low political profile at the WTO) is quite interesting, considering how they keep touting what strong proponents they are of the WTO and how their broad shoulders are up to the Sisyphean task of pushing the WTO up the hill," said a foreign trade expert.
Sisyphus was a mythological king of Corinth who was condemned to roll a heavy rock up a hill only to have it roll down again as it neared the top.
